description: We are Team GOAT, a multidisciplinary team passionate about data science, artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and space exploration. For this challenge, we aim to develop an AI-powered platform that identifies and evaluates locations on Earth with environmental and geological characteristics similar to the Moon and Mars.
summary:
Our project explores a way to identify Earth locations that could serve as analogs for lunar terrain. We developed an initial analysis pipeline and map that compare the Rima Hadley region of the Moon with 2,000 grid cells in Jordan’s Harrat al-Shaam volcanic field. Using open space data, including NASA’s LRO and Terra MODIS products, we ranked the cells by five characteristics: elevation range, slope, roughness, reflectance, and surface temperature difference. The map shows where promising candidates are and which characteristics drive their ranking.

This addresses the challenge by turning planetary and Earth observations into an explainable shortlist for further study. Such a tool could help researchers focus field visits and mission simulations on relevant terrain. Our results are preliminary: the ranked cells still need to be checked against known analog sites and independently validated.
details:
Project Details (English, ready to paste):

Our project is a prototype for finding Earth locations that may be useful analogs for lunar terrain. We tested it by comparing the Rima Hadley region of the Moon with Jordan’s Harrat al-Shaam volcanic field. A Python pipeline divides the Earth study area into 2,000 grid cells, calculates terrain and surface characteristics for each cell, and produces a ranked table and preliminary heatmap.

The comparison uses five characteristics: elevation range, slope, roughness, reflectance, and surface temperature difference. We used NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA and Diviner products for the lunar reference, NASA Terra MODIS for Earth temperature, and Copernicus DEM and Sentinel-2 for Earth terrain and imagery. The code uses Python libraries including NumPy, pandas, Rasterio, SciPy, and Matplotlib. We also adjusted the terrain data to more comparable spatial scales before calculating the rankings.

The project’s creative contribution is an explainable screening process: researchers can inspect the measurements and sources behind a candidate’s rank instead of relying on visual resemblance alone. It could help teams narrow down locations for field studies, rover testing, and exploration simulations. In the current results, 1,891 cells pass an optical surface filter.

We considered data resolution, terrain type, surface coverage, and the limits of comparing two very different environments. The ranking is preliminary: its scores are values within our chosen model, not percentages of lunar similarity. Before claiming any newly identified analog site, we need to exclude known sites and independently validate the leading candidates.
